*Brahmayāmala* 4, 32–33.

B = TUL 403;

*Nh* = Nagoya CA50-1 (30v4–), paper, [number of] folios; *Nn*.
How is it that you, the son of one who out of delusion denied vast objects such as the earth, the oceans, and the mountains, are not capable of concealing even this small skull?
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme characteristics of a worthy recipient (*pātra*).
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain [the vessels]: those made of clay, those born of tortoise-shell, those made of bell-metal, and those made of copper or iron. (1)

Then, for that reason, the supreme characteristics of the vessel are correctly explained: [one made of] clay, born from tortoise-shell, and indeed [one made of] bell-metal, born of bronze, and born of iron.
[It may be] made of clay or likewise from a tortoise shell, or fashioned from bone,
copper, or iron; or else it may be made of gold, silver, mother-of-pearl, or conch shell.
[The mirror] may be produced from silver,
or even from pearl-oyster shell, conch shell, the excellent coconut, or likewise another made of glass. (2)
The best coconut, as well as another made of gold, or silver, or likewise conch or mother-of-pearl.
The supreme fruit of Bal-po-se’u, as well as other newly arisen [substances]:
the pomegranate (śṛṅgodbhava), wood and the like, and especially stone.
Wood and so forth,
stone—
whether in one piece, two pieces, or three, four, or five pieces. || 3 ||
A single piece,
four pieces, or five pieces; furthermore,
stone vessels are especially superior to those made of clay or wood.
One section and two sections, likewise three, four, and five;
it is proclaimed as having six sections, seven sections, and eight sections.

[It is] proclaimed as having eight sections: Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, women, and the mixed castes (varṇasaṃkara). 4. [The reading is] *brāhmaṇa-kṣatriya-vaiśya-* [emended], [with variants:

*brāhmaṇā-* in *Padminī*, *A*, *L*, *Nk*, *Nh*; *brāhmaṇā-* in *Ne*; *-kṣatriya-vaiśyaṃ ca* in *A*; *-kṣatriyā-vaiśya-* in *L*; *kṣatriyā vaiśyā* in *Ne*; *kṣatriyo vaiśyaṃ* in *Nk*; *kṣatriyo vaiśya-* in *Nh*.
[Regarding the mixed castes of Śūdra women:
It is well known as the sixth, seventh, and eighth sections.
[They are those] born from women of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes at the end of their respective lineages.
White, red, white-and-red, dark-blue, yellow, and tawny; [white = Brāhmaṇa; red-and-white = Kṣatriya; yellow-and-tawny = Vaiśya; dark-blue = Śūdra; ash-colored and so forth are all Antyajās].
[He is] tawny (*piṅgala*);
[these forms] are proclaimed as ash-colored (*bhasmavarṇa*), discolored (*vivarṇa*), and multicolored (*nānāvarṇa*).
And they are proclaimed to be of various colors:
white, red, greenish-white, yellow, and likewise yellowish-white.
Renowned for ash-colored skin, a foul complexion, and various other complexions;
likewise, having deficient or extra teeth, and possessing various forms.
% \padmini most likely has cārdraṃ ca for cāntaṃ ca!
% [She is] beautiful, \padmini % [her] form is of various kinds] \L\Ne, [but] rutpannādhividhas \A, [her] own form is of various modes \Nk.
The double-layered, the elephant-back, the thunderbolt, and likewise the crow’s foot.
Superior, inferior, and lowest; likewise, there are various distinctions of shape.
Two depressions like the back of an elephant, or likewise the feet of a vajra or a crow;
teeth that are dark green or yellow, as well as broken and shattered.
Having observed all of this— whether it be dark, yellow, or having dark teeth, or yellow teeth— one should cause an examination to be conducted therein.
Having thus observed that,
[one should perform] the examination of the lotus-lake.
Whether it be green or yellow, or eaten by worms or maggots—
having observed all of this, one should thoroughly examine that place.
On whatever spot of earth it may be, whether it be soft or even dusty...
In a well-levelled region of earth,
at a site designated for the binding of the ritual enclosure, one should perform the rite with a mantra; there, one should observe its descent.
The minister should accomplish it— that is, he should seize it.
He should effect its attainment.
[The falling]:
On level ground, or in plains or sandy valleys,
the mantrin should perform the rite there and examine its falling.
One who has killed a Brahmin or a cow falls facing south; one who has killed a Brahmin or a cow falls toward the southwest.
One who kills a cow falls [into hell]; in the southwest (nairṛta) is one devoid of caste, and in the northwest (vāyavya) is a breaker of mantras.

In the western [direction], [it is] *vāruṇyām* according to A, *varuṇe* according to L, *vāruṇam* according to Ne, and *vāruṇyam* according to Nk; *varṇahīnam* according to Padminī, A, Ne, and Nk, while L has *hīnam*; and *ca* according to A, L, and Nk, while Ne has *tu*.
[Regarding *varṇahīnam*, Padminī understands it as "bringing dishonor.
In the northwestern [direction], [it is] *vāyavyām* according to A and Ne, *vāyuvye* according to L, and *vāyavyam* according to Nk.
If one looks toward the east, the Brahmins will be terrified;
by falling into the direction of the Vetalas (the South-East), cattle, those of no caste, and those of low birth will be afraid; and if one looks toward the northwest, the mantras will be endangered.
Facing north is sovereignty; in the northeast is that which bestows the accomplishment of mantras.
In the east, one who has heard the vow of non-violence should offer an oblation to the mouth of Agni.

...the one who destroys [obstacles], the proclaimer of vows, O Padminī; the one who moves through the self, the one who hears the primordial vow, the one who possesses vigor, the one who does not destroy, the proclaimer of vows—
[he is] the one whose face is turned toward Agni.

Looking toward the north, one will become wealthy; there is the accomplishment of mantras through mastery, and one’s ascetic observances (*vrata*) remain unimpaired. Looking toward the southeast, one becomes a plunderer;
the thief is indeed face-down, while the killer of women stands facing upward.
And the thief [is placed] face-down;
the slayer of a woman [is likewise].
If it falls on the side facing upward, it should be known as the characteristic of a *caṇḍāla* bowl.

...on the side: *caṇḍālaṃ* (the outcaste). It should be known as the characteristic [of the following]: "Likewise, one who looks downward is a thief; one who looks upward, by remaining [there], destroys women."
Because it has fallen into the logs, it is *caṇḍālī*; it should be known as having the characteristics of a vessel.
With one piece there is a *pīṭha*, and with two pieces it is the Lord of the Maṇḍala (*maṇḍaleśvara*).

He should be a *pīṭha* [one who is untiring in wandering through the *padminī*, i.e., the *pīṭhas* and so forth]; he should be a *maṇḍaleśvara*. The *trikhaṇḍa* [bestows] the accomplishment of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the accomplishment of mantra; it consists of four parts.

The three-sectioned [mantra] bestows the accomplishment of the practitioner; the four-part [mantra] grants mastery over the mantra. The single-stemmed [vase] confers power over the abode; the two-stemmed [vase] confers power over the maṇḍala.
Through three sections, the practitioner attains *siddhi*; through four sections, the *siddhi* of mantra;

through five sections, peace (*śānti*) and nourishment (*puṣṭi*)—the supreme accomplishment for the reciter. [śāntiḥ puṣṭiḥ pañcakhaṇḍaṃ mantriṇā siddhir uttamā |] [śāntiḥ puṣṭiḥ pañcakhaṇḍaṃ] \A, śāntipuṣṭiṃ tu pañcame \L\Ne, śāntipustiṃ tu paśvaṃma \Nk
Through the minister, supreme accomplishment is attained;
one should know the six-sectioned [mantra] for alms-seeking, while the seven-sectioned is for subjugation.
The *bhaikṣaka* (the one who obtains alms) is to be known as the one who effects the attainment of alms (*bhikṣālābhakṛt*). As for the *khaṇḍa*, it is used for subjugation (*vaśyaka*).
Through the five [limbs], there is pacification and enrichment.
One knows that the six pieces are obtained through begging; with seven pieces, one brings [others] under control.
Likewise, one should avoid the eight pieces, for the accomplishment of siddhi would be fruitless.

Brahmā should have one ear, and a Kṣatriya should have two ears. [The practice of propitiating deities] such as Śānti and others is fruitless without the means of accomplishment (*sādhananiṣphala*); however, this is acceptable for *krūra* rites. [According to the *Padminī*, it is fruitless without the means of accomplishing supernatural powers (*siddhisādhananiṣphala*).]

*Padminī*: “He would become one with a single ear. *A*, *L*, *Ne*: *ekaśrotraṃ*; *Nk*: *ekasrotaṃ* / *ekaśrota*. *Bhaved*: *L*, *Ne*, *Nk*: *bhaved*; *A*: *bhavyad*. *Brahmā*: *A*, *L*, *Ne*: *brahmā*; *Nk*: *brahma*.
One with a single ear.

Because the accomplishment of *siddhi* would be fruitless, one should likewise avoid the eight-petaled [mandala]. That which has one aperture becomes a Brahmin; that which has two apertures becomes a Kṣatriya.
The Vaiśya should be known as having three ears, while the two Śūdras have four ears.
Whether it lacks ears or has many ears, [such a person] should be avoided by the wise, even if they are of the Śūdra caste.
*asrotraṃ* (A, L, Ne, Nk); *bahusrotraṃ* (L, Ne, Nk). *varjanīyaṃ* (A); *varjaṇīyā* (L, Ne, Nk). *vicakṣaṇaiḥ* (A); *vicakṣaṇaḥ* (L, Ne, Nk).
The third opening is the *rājanya* (royal caste); the fourth opening is the *vaiśya* (commoner caste).
One with many openings or no openings at all should be avoided by the wise.
[If it should be very small in body and of yellowish color...]
One should not take a skull belonging to a woman, especially one that has fallen from its caste.
Those with missing teeth, those with no teeth, and those who are ungraspable are excluded from auspicious festivals.
And [they are] ungraspable; *śubhotsave* (in the auspicious festival). [Should one ask: "By a desire for what is auspicious?
Women and skull-cups are not to be grasped, especially those that have lost their color.
One who desires merit should not wear [teeth] that are missing or decayed; likewise,
one with darkened teeth, one with many afflictions, or one with teeth like the feet of a crow.
With the *kalikā* and *kāpada* [arrangements], there will indeed be violence (*hiṃsā*); likewise, with the *dvipuṭa* and *gajapṛṣṭha*, there is that which arises from disease (*vyādhi*).
If there is injury, it will indeed occur;
on the back of an elephant, there will be much suffering from disease, and there will be conflict with those of mixed bird-like feet.
The second hollow will lead to misfortune; likewise, within the back of the elephant [there is disease].
The *kāmadhenu* is seen in the center of the four depressions.
In the middle, and then before those two, that which is low is known as the Cintāmaṇi.
Before that, [the ground] is low-lying;
it is remembered as the *cintāmaṇi*. It is called the *cintāmaṇi*. It is remembered.
In the central region, there are four hollows; one should look toward the interval between the "Bestower of Desires.
In the front direction, there are two hollows, which are explained as being called the "Wish-Fulfilling Jewel" (*cintāmaṇi*).
It has the luster of a conch shell, jasmine, or the moon; it is very smooth and beautiful to behold.
It is as smooth as a jasmine flower or the moon;
beautiful and bestowing success upon all mantras, the practitioner shall attain accomplishment.
[The one who grants] the accomplishment of mantras;
one should look upon the auspicious [deity], whose color is like that of a conch, a *kunda* flower, or the moon, and who is glossy.
He bestows the accomplishments (*siddhi*) of all mantras and causes the practitioner to attain accomplishment. He has a large body of yellow color, the luster of a lotus, and the lotus as his emblem.
Radiant as a lotus,
marked with the sign of a lotus—
this is declared to be auspicious for rites of nourishment (*pauṣṭika*); through it, prosperity is accomplished.
It is praised for rites of enrichment (*pauṣṭika*); it is said [to be suitable] when [the practitioner] is cheerful, his complexion is yellow, or he resembles a lotus and is marked by a lotus;
through this, the attainment of abundant wealth is accomplished.
A vessel that is red in color, or else marked with red spots.
In the Great Time of subjugation and attraction, these are the characteristics of a worthy vessel that grant success.
At the time of subjugation and attraction, Mahākāla, whatever vessel is red in color and further marked by red *bindu*s—
The characteristics of a vessel that bestows the siddhis of constant mastery and summoning are as follows:
there should be a very firm [vessel] resembling a cow’s mouth (*gomukha*), and it should be provided with a ring (*muktikā*).
[It is] very firm; *muktikā* [is] born from oyster shell (*śuktija*),
and it is especially recommended for killing (*māraṇa*), driving away (*uccāṭana*), and causing enmity (*vidveṣa*).
For killing, expulsion, and inciting hatred—
specifically,
[the vessel] should have a shape like a *ba-laṅ-kha* (ox-head), be very firm, and be adorned with pearls.
It is especially praised for killing, expelling, and causing division.
When the worthy recipient has been obtained, it is excellent, bestowing the fruit of all desires.
O Goddess, the practitioner should accomplish [the goal] and wander through the sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and fields (*kṣetra*).
One should accept this [place],
complete with these characteristics, and thereby attain success.
One should take [it] in its entirety; one attains accomplishment.
One attains the highly praised vessel and bestows all desired fruits;
having traveled to the sacred sites and fields, the practitioner should accomplish the goddess.
When these characteristics are fully perfected and maintained, one will attain siddhi.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, the Instruction on the Characteristics of Vessels, in the glorious *Samvarodaya-mahātantra*.
This is the fifteenth chapter, the section definitively teaching the characteristics of the vessel, from the *Śrīsaṃvarodayamahātantra*.
